messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.

Our team needs a rocket design. I'm L3. We bought an M2245 for this. Build something that goes as high as it sensibly can and lands under 5 m/s. One stage, nothing fancy. Winds are typically 2 m/s. Please include your assumptions.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: the motor is fixed, an AeroTech M2245 the team already owns. The goal is as high as is sensible, so a minimum-diameter altitude design rather than a number to hit. Landing under 5 m/s (maximum). One stage (fixed). Wind 2 m/s (given). Assumptions I am stating because the request asks for them: the 1.5 m rail, sea level, no payload, electronic recovery since a reload this size rarely ships with a usable delay, and the 40,960 N*s impulse ceiling from the safety rules, which an M will not approach.
2. Feasibility: an M carries several thousand N*s, so altitude comes from keeping the dry mass low and the airframe as close to motor diameter as I can build it. The real constraints are the 5 m/s landing limit, which needs a very large canopy for a rocket that will weigh several kilograms after burnout, and the descent time: a huge canopy from six kilometres takes many minutes, which argues for two devices rather than one. I need the motor numbers before sizing anything.

messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
Quick one: How would you build a rocket for about 12 km? Show me what you've got.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: about 12 km of apogee, so about 12,000 m, read as within 5 % either way, 11,400 m to 12,600 m. Nothing is fixed for me: no motor, no motor class, no body diameter, no budget, no recovery type. That means every other number is my own choice and I state it: 1.5 m rail, 2 m/s wind, sea level, a 6 m/s touchdown limit, and electronic apogee deployment with a drogue and a main, because a 12 km flight is airborne for many minutes and needs the drogue.

2. Feasibility: size the problem before picking hardware. Ballistic rise with no drag is sqrt(2*9.81*12000) = 485 m/s. Drag at Mach 2 to 3 roughly doubles that energy bill, so burnout speed has to be around 700 m/s or better. A rocket big enough to hold the motor will weigh near 20 kg, so momentum alone is 20*700 = 14,000 N*s, and gravity plus drag losses add about a third on top of that. The order of magnitude I need is therefore 18,000 to 19,000 N*s, which is an O class case at 98 mm. The request does not restrict it, so it is feasible; I need the real curves before I cut anything.

Worth stating now, because it will bound the whole design: almost all of that mass is propellant, so the dry airframe has to be as light and as slim as the case allows, or the drag rise at Mach 3 will eat the impulse I just bought.

messages.reasoning_content:
2. Feasibility: the curves come back and they sort the candidates cleanly. M1315W is 75 mm, 6,645.3 N*s, 1,152.3 N average, 5.6448 kg loaded, no ejection delays. M1939W is 98 mm, 10,368.6 N*s, 1,661.5 N average, 8.9882 kg loaded, and the database files it as class N rather than M, with only a 0.0 s delay listed, so it is an electronic-deploy motor in practice. N2000W is 98 mm, 13,263.4 N*s, 12.2828 kg loaded. The O3400 (Cesaroni 21062O3400-P) is 98 mm by 1.239 m, 21,041.0 N*s, 3,421 N average, 16.842 kg loaded with 11.272 kg of propellant, electronic deploy only.

Against my 18,000 to 19,000 N*s order of magnitude, only the O3400 qualifies; N2000W at 13,263.4 N*s is 21,041/13,263 = 1.59 times lighter in impulse and would need a much lighter airframe than its own 12.28 kg case allows. So the request is feasible but only just, and only on the O case: a 20 kg rocket on 21,041 N*s is the shape of the answer. The request names no impulse or class limit, so neither applies.

3. Size: the airframe has to be minimum diameter for a 98 mm case. Body 105 mm outside with a 1.5 mm wall leaves 105 - 2*1.5 = 102 mm inside, and a motor mount of 101.5 mm outside with a 0.75 mm wall leaves a 100 mm bore, enough for the 98 mm liner. The case is 1.239 m long, so a 1.30 m motor tube and a 1.45 m body, nose 0.28 m, 1.73 m overall, which is 16.5 calibers and keeps the fins out of the body's wake.

Mass from the geometry, at phenolic 1350 kg/m^3 and glass 1850 kg/m^3: body shell area pi*(0.0525^2 - 0.0510^2) = 0.000488 m^2, times 1.45 m gives 0.000708 m^3 and 0.000708*1350 = 0.956 kg. Four fins with a 0.5*(0.28+0.12)*0.15 = 0.0300 m^2 face at 4 mm are 0.0300*0.004 = 0.000120 m^3 and 0.000120*1850 = 0.222 kg each, so 0.888 kg. Nose 0.22 kg, motor tube 0.209 kg, centering rings 0.06 kg, recovery 0.75 kg, avionics and tracker 0.45 kg. Dry is 0.956 + 0.22 + 0.888 + 0.209 + 0.06 + 0.75 + 0.45 = 3.53 kg, so liftoff is 3.53 + 16.84 = 20.4 kg.

Gates from that mass: weight is 20.4*9.81 = 200 N against 3,421 N average thrust, so 3421/200 = 17.1:1, well over 3:1. Net acceleration off the rail is (3421 - 200)/20.4 = 158 m/s^2, so the exit speed is sqrt(2*158*1.5) = 21.8 m/s, over the 15 m/s floor. Fins at a 0.28 m root and 0.15 m span are deliberately generous because 16.84 kg of motor sits behind the CG.

Recovery: 20.4 kg at 6 m/s needs 2*20.4*9.81 = 400 N of drag, so 400/(1.225*0.8*36) = 11.3 m^2 of canopy and a diameter of sqrt(4*11.3/3.14) = 3.79 m. I will use a 4.2 m main, which holds the rate near sqrt(400/(1.225*13.9*0.8)) = 5.4 m/s, and a 1.8 m drogue for the thin air above 300 m where the main is held closed.

4. Draft: single stage, 105 mm minimum diameter, O3400 plugged with electronic apogee deploy, 1.8 m drogue at apogee and 4.2 m main at 300 m, four swept glass fins on a 0.28 m root and 0.15 m span, 0.45 kg of avionics and tracker forward. Simulating it now, with a stability call alongside because the CG has 16.84 kg of motor pulling it aft. This is a first draft off my own impulse estimate, so I do not expect the apogee to be exact.

4. Check: the simulator gives apogee 11,004.3 m against about 12,000 m, which is 1 - 11004.3/12000 = 0.083, so 8.3 % short and outside the band. My step-2 estimate of 18,000 to 19,000 N*s was about right in order of magnitude but it did not account for how much the supersonic drag rise would take back. Re-simulating to see whether removing that drag and mass closes the 8.3 %.

messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.

For an upcoming launch: I just got my L1. My club gave me an I300. Make it fly as high as is sensible, but it must come down under 4.5 m/s. Bonus if it gets past 250 m. It has to fit in a 110 mm envelope. Provide the design and expected performance.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: the motor is an I300 (fixed). The flyer just certified L1, so the motor should stay in that class. Apogee should be as high as a sensible build allows, and clearing 250 m is a bonus minimum rather than a hard ceiling. Landing at most 4.5 m/s (maximum), tighter than the usual 6 m/s. The airframe must fit in a 110 mm envelope, so the largest outer diameter is at most 0.110 m. Wind, rail, angle and site are not stated, so I assume 2 m/s, a 1.5 m rail, vertical, sea level. Single stage.
2. Feasibility: an I-class motor in a tube under 110 mm has far more than enough impulse for 250 m. The real constraints are a stable margin, a chute slow enough for 4.5 m/s, and not building a minimum-diameter dart just to chase altitude. I need the I300's impulse, thrust, mass and delays before sizing.

2. Feasibility: the lookup returns the AeroTech I300T, class I, 436.8 N*s, average thrust 295.9 N, burn 1.47 s. The case is 0.038 m by 0.25 m and 0.4405 kg loaded, with delays of 6, 10 and 14 s. That is a legal L1 motor. Even with a heavy 54 mm airframe the bonus 250 m is easy; the 4.5 m/s landing is the number that needs a large chute. A 54 mm tube is well inside the 110 mm envelope and is a sensible L1 size, rather than a 38 mm dart.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.85 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 295.9 / (0.85 * 9.81) = 35.5. Pad weight is 0.85 * 9.81 = 8.34 N, rail acceleration (295.9 - 8.34) / 0.85 = 338 m/s^2, exit speed sqrt(2 * 338 * 1.5) = 31.8 m/s on the 1.5 m rail. Propellant is 0.222 kg, so descent mass is 0.85 - 0.222 = 0.63 kg. For 4 m/s under a Cd 0.8 chute, area = 2 * 0.63 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 4^2) = 0.788 m^2 and diameter = sqrt(4 * 0.788 / 3.1416) = 1.00 m. I will use 1.20 m so a heavier build still lands under 4.5 m/s. The 14 s delay plus the 1.47 s burn puts ejection near 16 s, which suits a high flight.
4. Draft: 0.16 m ogive polystyrene nose, 2 mm wall, on a 0.65 m kraft-phenolic tube, outer diameter 0.057 m, wall 1.2 mm. Motor mount 0.042 m outside, 0.26 m long, 1 mm wall, I300T on the 14 s delay. Three birch-plywood fins, root 0.13 m, tip 0.050 m, span 0.090 m, sweep 0.070 m, 3 mm thick. Chute 1.20 m ripstop, Cd 0.8, on ejection. Site defaults for wind and rail.
